interest: This file is valuable for historians studying the diplomatic and military rapprochement between Japan and Siam (Thailand) during the 1930s, between the Siamese revolution of 1932 and World War II. It documents how Japan utilized naval goodwill and training missions—such as the visits of the Kuma in 1934 and the training squadrons in 1935 and 1938—to project power and cultivate political influence. The documents highlight Japanese ideological rhetoric emphasizing commonalities such as constitutional monarchism, Buddhism, and a shared mission for 'peace in the Far East.' Furthermore, Minister Neville's report illuminates domestic tensions within Siam during the Second Sino-Japanese War, particularly official fears of anti-Japanese protests or sabotage by the local Chinese community, necessitating strict security measures like running pilot locomotives ahead of Japanese naval trains.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.3392) comprises U.S. State Department records from March 1934 to June 1938 concerning visits of Imperial Japanese Navy vessels and aircraft to ports in Thailand (Siam). The file includes cross-reference sheets, an extract report, an internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum, and a detailed diplomatic despatch from the American Legation in Bangkok. These records document three distinct naval visits: the cruiser Kuma in February 1934, whose officers participated in cremation ceremonies for Siamese soldiers killed in the 1933 Boworadet rebellion; a training squadron of the cruisers Asama and Yakumo under Rear Admiral Kamisaburo Nakamura in April 1935; and the training ships Iwate and Yakumo under Rear Admiral Shiro Takasu in May 1938, carrying approximately 400 naval cadets. Together, the papers capture the deepening political and military rapport between Japan and Siam, Japanese rhetoric emphasizing shared Buddhist heritage and constitutional systems, and the anxieties of Siamese authorities over potential anti-Japanese terrorism by the local Chinese population.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 40 from Siam regarding the visit of the Japanese cruiser Kuma to Bangkok.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Document File Note recording that Despatch No. 40, dated March 9, 1934, from Baker in Siam, is filed under decimal file 892.00 P.R./59. It records the subject as the visit of the Japanese cruiser Kuma at Bangkok on February 17, 1934. The sheet directs researchers to the periodic political report file.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Visit of Japanese Cruiser Kuma (Despatch No. 40)

subfiles.about: Report describing the visit of the Japanese cruiser Kuma to Bangkok and its participation in official ceremonies.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese 5,700-ton cruiser Kuma arrived outside the bar at Bangkok on February 17, 1934, timed to coincide with cremation ceremonies for soldiers killed during the recent Siamese rebellion. The Japanese naval delegation played a prominent role in the ceremonies, where the Japanese national anthem was performed, and attended exclusive bilateral social events at the Japanese Legation. Foreign residents in Bangkok were also surprised by a Japanese naval seaplane flying low over the city during the visit.
subfiles.title: Report on the Visit of Japanese Cruiser Kuma to Bangkok

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 210 regarding the arrival of a Japanese training squadron off Siam.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Document File Note indicating that Despatch No. 210, dated April 24, 1935, from Baker in Siam, is filed under 892.00 P.R./72. It records the arrival of the Japanese training squadron, composed of the cruisers Asama and Yakumo, off the bar of the Menam River. The squadron was under the command of Rear Admiral Kamisaburo Nakamura.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Visit of Japanese Training Squadron (Despatch No. 210)

subfiles.about: Department of State memorandum summarizing Bangkok Despatch No. 171 on the visit of Japanese training ships to Bangkok.
subfiles.summary: John H. Spencer of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Despatch No. 171 from Bangkok concerning the visit of Japanese training ships Iwate and Yakumo from May 18 to May 24, 1938. The memo notes the presence of about 400 naval cadets from Tokyo and highlights the commanding officer's statement regarding a shared mission for peace in the Far East, constitutional government, and similar religions. It also reports the squadron's donation of 1,500 baht to hospitals in Lopburi and Sattahip and observes minimal public reaction in Siam.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Japanese Training Ships Visit

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on the goodwill visit of Japanese training ships Iwate and Yakumo to Siam.
subfiles.summary: American Minister Edwin L. Neville reports on the visit of the Japanese training ships Iwate and Yakumo under Rear Admiral Takasu, which anchored off Paknam from May 18 to May 24, 1938. The complement of approximately 1,000 officers, crew, and 400 naval cadets visited Bangkok and were hosted at Lopburi for an elephant hunt, while Admiral Takasu issued a public statement emphasizing mutual friendship, constitutional government, Buddhism, and Far Eastern peace. Neville notes the officers donated money to hospitals in Lopburi and Sattahip, and mentions that Siamese authorities operated a pilot engine ahead of the cadets' train due to rumors of Chinese anti-Japanese terrorism.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 171 from Bangkok on Visit of Japanese Training Ships

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 186 reporting on the visit of Japanese naval vessels Iwate and Yakumo.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Document File Note recording that Despatch No. 186, dated June 18, 1938, from Neville in Siam, is located under 892.00 P.R./110. It references an additional report concerning the visit of the two Japanese naval vessels, Iwate and Yakumo (recorded as Yakuno), to Bangkok. The document was indexed under State Department decimal file 894.3392/5.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Report of Japanese Naval Vessels Visit (Despatch No. 186)
